42.0.0.en: 1- “As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.”

42.0.1.en: The hart: the buck of the mountain goat, resembling the gazelle.

42.0.2.en: 1- The hart is swift in movement and attacks snakes, kills them and eats them, which makes its inside hot, and it needs to drink much water, and if it does not drink it is exposed to destruction, so the hart longs greatly to drink water.

42.0.3.en: 2- As the hart is marked by its inclination to drink water, so the writer of the psalm feels that his soul longs for God and cannot live without Him, and will perish if it does not find Him.

42.1.0.en: 2- “My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God?”

42.1.1.en: 1- The writer of the psalm feels that he longs for God, and man cannot live without drinking. So he is in spiritual thirst for God, and describes God as living to distinguish Him from the dead pagan gods, which are idols that do not move, for God is the source of life.

42.1.2.en: 2- The longing of the writer of the psalm is not to pray to God in just any place, but to appear before Him, that is, in His temple in Jerusalem, because the writer is estranged from Jerusalem. This shows the importance of prayer in the Church, in addition to prayer in every place.

42.2.0.en: 3- “My tears have been my bread day and night, while they say unto me every day, Where is thy God?”

42.2.1.en: 1- The enemies reproached the writer of the psalm that his God had left him, since he is estranged from Jerusalem, expelled and exiled, so he is in affliction and God has not helped him. So they make him doubt the existence of his God, or the power of his God to rescue him.

42.2.2.en: 2- The faith of the writer of the psalm was not shaken, but he continued in his prayers by day and by night, and his prayers were from his heart, so they were mingled with his tears, which express his longings for God and his grief over the affliction from which he suffers. So longings and griefs were mingled together in a wonderful way, and were mingled also with his faith, so his prayers continued. And he was not distracted from these prayers by talking with people, or by the works of life that are done in the daytime, nor did they stop with sleep during the night. Rather the longings of his heart continued, and covered everything in the day and the night. And from the excess of his sense of the importance of prayer and tears they became necessary to his life like bread, so that he cannot do without them. And he said “my bread” and not my water; for whoever eats bread while thirsty, his thirst increases; likewise the more his prayers and tears continue, the more his longing toward God increases.

42.3.0.en: 4- “When I remember these things, I pour out my soul upon me: for I used to pass along with the throng, I went in procession with them to the house of God, with the voice of joy and praise, a multitude keeping holyday.”

42.3.1.en: I pour out my soul upon me: I meditate and look deeply into myself and pray with fervor and tears.

42.3.2.en: I go in procession: I go up the steps of the mountains leading to the temple.

42.3.3.en: The throng: the congregation of worshipers.

42.3.4.en: 1- When his enemies reproached him they increased his present griefs, so he remembered the past days in which he enjoyed being in the temple of God. And he did not remember them with a feeling of deprivation and despair, but with the hope that he would return and enjoy them. For although there are griefs in the present, his past enjoyment stirred in him longings for the future, to enjoy worship in the temple of God.

42.3.5.en: 2- When he remembered the past joys he poured out his soul upon himself, and was not enraged at his enemies who drove him out, but turned to meditation and prayer deep within, so he rejoiced in God's past blessings and longed for them, and his prayers became satisfying to his soul.

42.3.6.en: 3- The writer remembered when he used to go up the mountain with the congregation of believers to worship in the temple of God, and he would lead them in beautiful songs, perhaps the Psalms of Ascents (Ps 120-134).

42.4.0.en: 5- “Why art thou bowed down, O my soul? and why dost thou groan within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him for the salvation of his countenance.”

42.4.1.en: 1- David, or the writer of the psalm, reproaches his own soul because it was bowed down, or broken and weakened, before the reproach of the enemies, who said to it “Where is thy God.” Indeed from the abundance of distress it came to groan and ache, and this does not agree with faith and hope in God; the soul must bear affliction with contentment and steadfastness in faith. So the problem is in his soul because of the weakness of its faith, for if it were steadfast in faith it would not have weakened before the reproaches of the enemies.

42.4.2.en: 2- He calls to his soul to hope in God, and David reveals the sweet side within him that struggles with the groaning, so he says, I still praise God and thank Him for all that He allows for me, even if it is affliction. And I see the face of God, so I see my salvation which must be accomplished, and this affliction ends; indeed my preoccupation with my spiritual salvation lifts me above the toils of the affliction so that I forget them.

42.4.3.en: It is good that you review yourself every day to discover your weaknesses and recover your faith and your spiritual principles, so that you return to God by repentance, and raise up your soul, to live with God and enjoy fellowship with Him.

42.5.0.en: 6- “O my God, my soul is bowed down within me: therefore will I remember thee from the land of Jordan, and of the Hermonites, from the hill Mizar.”

42.5.1.en: The mountains of Hermon: mountains that extend from the north toward the south and in which are the sources of the River Jordan, and the mountains are called “Sirion” (Deut 3:9; Ps 29:6) or “Senir” (Deut 3:9) or “Sion” (Deut 4:48). They are high mountains, whose height is nine thousand two hundred feet above sea level, and they have three peaks. And these mountains lie north of Palestine, where the tribe of Dan dwells, and in ancient times were the possession of Og king of Bashan.

42.5.2.en: Mount Mizar: one of the peaks of the mountains of Hermon.

42.5.3.en: When David found his soul still bowed down within him, he treated it by taking refuge with God, so he remembered God in his exile, which was at the sources of the River Jordan, the mountains of Hermon and Mount Mizar. And by remembering God he began to regain the strength of his faith, and hope revived within him. And because he was in affliction he was humble when he prayed to God, so he obtained divine grace and spiritual support.

42.6.0.en: 7- “Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy currents and thy billows have covered me.”

42.6.1.en: Deep: deep waters that cover whoever enters them.

42.6.5.en: 1- David in his exile at the sources of the River Jordan saw the overwhelming waters following one another as they came down from the mountains of Hermon, where the snow melts and the waters flow with force; indeed he heard the strong sound of the waterfalls, and saw the waves dashing and covering everything in their path. So he meditated on them and saw that in this affliction of his it was as though his soul were in the midst of the River Jordan, and these waters, currents and waves were coming upon him, so he felt that they express what he suffers in his affliction.

42.6.6.en: 2- It is beautiful that David feels that all that happens to him is by divine arrangement, so he accepted it from the hand of God in submission, and at the same time he had a firm hope that God would lift from him all that he suffers during his affliction.

42.7.0.en: 8- “In the daytime the LORD commands his mercy, and in the night his praise is with me, a prayer to the God of my life.”

42.7.1.en: 1- David feels that he enjoys all day long the mercy of God, which He commands His angels to pour out upon men, and especially His children; therefore he thanks God for His mercy, but in the night, when people sleep and life grows quiet, David devotes himself to praising God, to whom his heart clung, until he felt that God is his life, so he continues all night praising God, as the Fathers said, “The night is set apart for prayer.” So David prays to God by day and by night; because He is his life, so in the daytime he awaits His mercy, and in the night he praises Him for these mercies.

42.7.2.en: 2- The night is a symbol of the life we live on earth, for it is darkness when measured against eternity, where we do not see God except as in a mirror, as the Apostle Paul said (2 Cor 3:18). And in this night David praises all his life. But the day, which is a symbol of eternity, in it David obtains the mercies of God, who commands His angels to give him to enjoy his life with them.

42.7.3.en: 3- The day is also a symbol of life in the light of God, for God supports His children with His mercies in their striving to speak to Him, and these mercies continue all day long. But the night is a symbol of the wars of the devil, who wants to make us fall into sin, during which we do not see God as in the daytime, but we do not stop our praise of God; because He is our life, without whom we cannot live.

42.8.0.en: 9- “I will say unto God my rock, Why hast thou forgotten me? why go I mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?”

42.8.1.en: David, who enjoys fellowship with God by day and night, trusts that God is his rock, and his strong support able to rescue him, but he suffers pains in the affliction, which he expresses by saying why hast thou forgotten me and why do I mourn because of the reproaches of my enemy. He is not despairing, or doubting God's support of him, but he expresses his severe pains, as Christ on the Cross expressed the depth of His pains by saying, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mt 27:46).

42.9.0.en: 10- “With a crushing in my bones my oppressors reproach me, saying to me every day, Where is thy God. 11- Why art thou bowed down, O my soul, and why dost thou groan within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.” The reproaches of David's enemies were very severe during his affliction, and they made him doubt that God had left him because he is wicked, so that his spirit was crushed within him, and he expressed this by saying that his bones were crushed; because the bones are the strong part that gives the body firmness and rigidity, especially as the enemies continued to reproach him, so the crushing continued in the bones. But his hope was still strong in God; because he called to his soul that was bowed down and broken within him not to groan but to hope in God, as we explained earlier in the verse (v. 5).

42.9.1.en: Do not let afflictions keep you from God, but continue in your prayers and your praise of Him, confident of His love for you and His nearness to you, and that He will intervene at the right time with great power.

42.9.2.en: The glories of the King and the Queen. To the choirmaster “according to the Lilies.” For the sons of Korah. A poem. A song of love “My heart overflows with a good matter” (v. 1) Introduction:

42.9.4.en: A - The sons of Korah, as is written in the title of the psalm.

42.9.5.en: B - David, and he gave it to the sons of Korah so that they might chant it, and this is the more probable opinion.

42.9.6.en: 2- The psalm was chanted “according to the Lilies,” as in the title of the psalm, and what is meant by the lilies:

42.9.9.en: 3- This psalm is Messianic, because it speaks clearly about the Messiah the King.

42.9.10.en: 4- This psalm speaks about the Incarnation of Christ; therefore it is read on the Feast of the Nativity in the Hoos of the feast.

42.9.11.en: 5- This psalm also speaks about the bride, who is:

42.9.14.en: C - The human soul that loves Christ.

42.9.15.en: 6- This psalm is a song of love as in its title; because it is praise and love of God, then a love offered to the Church that clings to Christ.

42.9.16.en: 7- This psalm shows the greatness of life with God, and His children's enjoyment of blessings on earth and glories in heaven.

42.9.17.en: 8- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Third Hour, when the Holy Spirit descends upon the Church and gives her to enjoy glory with her Bridegroom, Christ the King.

43.0.0.en: 1- “Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against a nation that is merciless: O deliver me from the deceitful and unjust man.”

43.0.1.en: 1- David cries for help to the just God to judge in the circumstances through which he is passing, which are the agitation of Saul with his whole kingdom trying to kill David; indeed he asks God to stand as an adversary in his place before Saul who contends with him, to ward off from him every evil that Saul tries to direct. And David's asking for God's meeting shows:

43.0.2.en: A - David's faith in God who loves him and shepherds him.

43.0.3.en: B - David's uprightness, so that he is not afraid of God's judgment and justice, for he is wronged, and cries to God for help.

43.0.4.en: C - He did not mention the name of his enemy who wrongs him, and this shows God's kindness. For he wants nothing but God's defense of him, and protection from the evil coming upon him, although he is innocent.

43.0.5.en: 2- This verse applies to Christ, whom the scribes and Pharisees tried to trap in some error, and the priests tried to kill, and stirred up the nation of the Jews against Him, until they crucified Him in the end, aided by the treacherous, deceitful disciple Judas Iscariot, who is “the deceitful and unjust man.”

43.0.6.en: 3- This verse also applies to the Church, against which the world rises and which it persecutes, and some try to flatter her with deceit to reach evil goals. So the Church asks God to rescue her from the wicked and from the evil world surrounding her.

43.1.0.en: 2- “For thou art the God of my strength: why hast thou cast me off? why go I mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?”

43.1.1.en: David believes that God is his protection and his permanent fortress. This reassures David's heart, but he asks why God rejected him, since by his flight from Saul he went far away and was deprived of offering worship in the temple of God, and this led to grief in his heart. Therefore he asks God, “Have you forgotten me? Or how does your protection of me and your love agree with your depriving me of worshiping you in your temple?!” And this matter, that is, God's setting David aside and neglecting him, pained David's heart greatly; therefore he repeated it in many psalms such as (Ps 3; 10; 73). But despite David's grief he did not lose his hope, for he walked on, that is, he continued in his life and spiritual striving until God lifted these griefs from him.

43.2.0.en: 3- “O send out thy light and thy truth: let them lead me; let them bring me unto thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles.”

43.2.1.en: 1- The light of God and His truth, that is, His justice, is the Holy Spirit, who enlightens David's life and supports him in his affliction, since he is wronged, and prepares his way to return to the holy hill of God and His dwellings, that is, the Tabernacle, to enjoy the worship of God. And the hill of God is Mount Zion, on which the city of Jerusalem was built. And the writer says His dwellings, because in the days of David there were two dwellings of God: the first dwelling, or the first tent, in Jerusalem, in which was the Ark of the Covenant, and the second tent in the city of Gibeon, in which were the rest of the contents of the Tabernacle (1 Chr 16:37-39). And David says “let them lead me and bring me” because David was walking sad, continuing his striving, but he was unable to reach the temple of God except with the help of the Holy Spirit.

43.2.2.en: 2- The light and the truth are Christ, who said, I am the way, the truth and the life, and said, I am the light of the world. And by His redemption He brings up all mankind that believes in Him, to enjoy worship in His Church, and after this brings them up to the heavenly Jerusalem, to the Kingdom of Heaven.

43.2.3.en: 3- The prophets in the Old Testament await the Messiah, who is the light and the truth, to lead them with all mankind, to enjoy His redemption and His salvation which He accomplished on the Cross.

43.3.0.en: 4- “Then I will go to the altar of God, to God the gladness of my joy, and I will praise thee with the harp, O God my God. 5- Why art thou bowed down, O my soul, and why dost thou groan within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.”

43.3.1.en: 1- When David comes to the temple of God and His altar he can be free of his griefs; because he enjoys seeing God in his worship, and this is what makes him glad and joyful. He has no joy in the world and all that is in it, but his joy is only in God, who comforts his heart for all he has borne of pains. And then he can sing to God with the harp; for how can he sing and rejoice far from God, as the captives in Babylon felt, so they said, How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land (Ps 137:4).

43.3.2.en: 2- David asks his soul, after this hope of rejoicing in the hands of God in His temple; and says, why art thou bowed down, O my soul, and groanest within me, hold fast to God your hope, who will compensate you for all your toils (see the explanation of Ps 42:5).

43.3.3.en: May you look to Christ, your hope and your joy, when you pass through any affliction or griefs, and know that they are temporary, and after them Christ will compensate you with a peace and consolation that fills your heart, which cannot be expressed. Meditate on His past love for you, which will overflow upon you shortly, and your soul will grow calm and be at rest.

43.3.4.en: Thanksgiving and a request for salvation. To the choirmaster. A psalm of David “I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me” (v. 1) Introduction:

43.3.7.en: A - The first opinion: at the end of the period of Saul's pursuit of him, that is, shortly before David's reign.

43.3.8.en: B - After David's victory over Absalom and his return to his throne.

43.3.9.en: 3- After bearing many pains David thanks God in this psalm, declaring his obedience to Him, and asking the continuance of His help. So it is a psalm of thanksgiving, suitable for the children of God when they feel God's work with them.

43.3.10.en: 4- This psalm is one of the Messianic psalms; because it speaks with many allusions about Christ.

43.3.11.en: 5- The Apostle Paul quoted from this psalm in his Epistle to the Hebrews (Heb 10:5-10).

43.3.12.en: 6- This psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.
